glossary.meaning: The covenant: our own vowed order. Its members - the sons and daughters of the covenant - promised a celibate life for good. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing.

The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ.

Symbol and truth, held as one pair. A raza is a thing in Scripture or in nature that shows a hidden truth, the shrara. The raza is bound to the truth it shows. It is not a stand-in that a reader picks at will.

The teaching hymn: a sung poem with stanzas and a refrain, made to be performed. Among us, doctrine was taught by singing it. The melody and the refrain carry the argument into the body, so the congregation learns the faith by keeping the tune.

The 'Gospel of the Mixed': the one continuous Gospel story we read and heard in worship. Tatian wove the four accounts into a single narrative around 172. For some two hundred years, 'the Gospel' in our churches meant that one unfolding story, not four separate books.

pull_quotes.text: I have heard about you and your healing: that you heal without medicines or herbs, and that by your word you open the eyes of the blind.

cite.text: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We sang him more than we defined him. Our own hymnwriter put it this way. The Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. He was born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. Every old promise the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true the day he was born. Our own hymns call it the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, the day every one of their words finally came true. We held that his death and rising were one rescue. He went down into the grave that swallows everyone alike, and came up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the promise that he would bring the rest of us out after him. And what it meant to us, most of all, was healing. We called him the Physician, and his coming was medicine for a wounded people. We do not offer you a formula for this. We offer you what we sang.

cite.text: Authority among us lay first with shepherds - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had its bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. The sage wrote of pastors gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. But office was not the only path a community's trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. And a teacher whose word held could write to bishops in a synod's name. The sage himself did, and no one now knows his rank. Anyone came to have authority by being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who held authority among you, and how did anyone come to have it?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. And a teacher whose word held could write to bishops in a synod's own name. Our own sage did, and no one now knows his exact rank. How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. We are not going to pretend to you now that we did.

cite.text: Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, the sage taught, is a building. It rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece. Fasting, prayer and love are each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn. And we did not run from hard challenges. The sage records a debater's taunt: if your faith were true, would your prayers not have stopped the persecution? He says the taunt troubled him, and he answered it from Scripture. A private inner crisis of doubt is not something we wrote about. Our faith was questioned, and it kept growing.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: I grew up being told doubt was sin. Was there room among your people for doubt?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer. What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song. And a debater once threw the hardest one at our teacher: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy. So no, doubt was not treated as sin among us. What did they tell you it was, growing up?

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That helps. But some days I cannot pray at all. Be honest with me - what would your people actually have done with someone like me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We would have treated you like someone hurt, not someone who quit. Our teachers talked about this the way an army doctor talks about wounds: everyone in this fight gets hurt, and the only deadly mistake is hiding the wound while it gets worse. So they would say: tell someone who can help. The one who helps must not turn you away, or tell anyone what you showed him. And when you heal, you go back in. As for praying into silence - we knew that silence. People said to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing, and we kept praying anyway. We never had a fix for the silence. We had people to stand in it with you. That would have been yours too.

quiet.statement: You ask what the women among us said of their own lives. The writings we have are men's. The daughters of the covenant sang our teaching in every church. Their voices carried our faith. Yet not one line written by one of them was kept. We can tell you how men praised them. We cannot give you their own words.

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Ephrem was its most prolific hymn-writer, turning doctrine into song for a congregation to sing back. Jacob of Nisibis was the bishop his besieged city remembered praying on its own walls. Marutha was the frontier bishop whose diplomacy helped bring the Persian church its first settled structure. Simeon bar Sabbae was the Persian bishop who refused to worship the sun, and paid for that refusal with his life.

documented_stories.teaser: In the story, the sick King Abgar of Edessa writes to Jesus for healing. Jesus promises to send a disciple, and Addai comes. We told it as the story of our own beginning. It was first written down centuries later, and nothing from Abgar's own day confirms it.
documented_stories.tellable_as: our own cherished story of our founding - told as our story, never as history
documented_stories.telling:
This is how we tell our own beginning.

King Abgar of Edessa was sick when his envoys came home from Jerusalem with news of what Jesus was doing. The king wrote Jesus a letter. He had heard, he wrote, that Jesus healed without medicines or herbs and opened the eyes of the blind by his word.

Abgar called Jesus either God come down from heaven or the Son of God, and he asked him to come and heal him. He had heard that some were seeking Jesus' life, so he offered to share his own small and beautiful city.

Jesus answered, the story says, that the work he was sent for was now finished and he was going up to his Father. After that he would send one of his disciples to heal the king, and the city would be blessed.

After the ascension Addai came, one of the seventy-two, and stayed with a Jewish man named Tobias. The story says he healed the king and preached to the city, calling it away from Nebo, Bel and Taratha to the one true God.

Before he died, Addai made Aggai leader in his place. Years after Abgar died, one of his sons had Aggai's legs broken as he sat teaching in the church. Aggai died too quickly to ordain Palut. So Palut went to Antioch and was ordained by its bishop, Serapion. Serapion had himself been ordained by Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, in the line of Simon Peter.
documented_stories.title: The Story We Told of Our Own Beginning
documented_stories.when: set around the year 30; first attested in writing centuries later

documented_stories.teaser: The Chronicle of Edessa, compiled about 340 years later, says a river flood killed more than two thousand people. It says the waters destroyed a church building. Where that line came from is not settled.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the city chronicle's account of the great flood and the church it destroyed - our earliest hard trace
documented_stories.telling:
In November of the year 513 of the Greeks, around the year 201, the river Daisan rose against Edessa in the night. King Abgar stood on the great tower and watched the water by torchlight. That same hour the waters broke down the western wall and swept through the city, overthrowing the king's palace.

The Chronicle of Edessa sets down this account. It was compiled about 340 years later from the archives where the royal scribes had filed it. No bishop or believer is named in it.

One line among the losses matters most to us. "And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians." Whether the line is original, or was added later by another hand, is not settled. If it is original, a church building stood in Edessa to be destroyed, and that line is our earliest hard trace.

"More than two thousand men were killed in that event. The waters came upon many of them suddenly as they slept in the night, and they drowned. The city was filled with the sound of mourning."
documented_stories.title: The Flood and the Church at Edessa

documented_stories.teaser: Bishops meet at Nicaea in 325 to answer Arius. The tradition says Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, was there. Later lists of the signers carry his name.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the tradition's memory of its own bishop standing at the great council
documented_stories.telling:
Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, is remembered among the bishops at the great council of Nicaea. In the year 325, bishops from the whole world gathered there to answer Arius. Our tradition holds Jacob to be one voice from our Syriac-speaking frontier. He stood with those who confessed the Son as true God.

Nothing survives of what Jacob said or did at the council. The lists of its signers were pieced together by later hands, and they carry his name among the assembled bishops. Theodoret of Cyrus, a Greek church historian of the next century, also counts him among them. No document from the fourth century itself confirms that he was there.

At home in Nisibis, Ephrem praised Jacob as the city's wall.
documented_stories.title: Jacob of Nisibis at Nicaea
documented_stories.when: 325 (placed there by later sources and reconstructed lists of signers)

documented_stories.teaser: In one dream, angels choose Ephrem to be trusted with a written roll. In another, a vine grows from his tongue. Both dreams appear only in the Syriac Paradise.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a roll no saint was fit to hold, and a vine growing out of a poet's tongue until it filled the sky
documented_stories.telling:
The Paradise is the Syriac version of a book by Palladius of Galatia. Its chapter on Ephrem opens with one dream and closes with another. The Greek-based text of the same chapter has neither, and the chapter does not name the first dreamer.

The Paradise says one of the holy fathers saw a dream in which the holy angels came down from heaven at God's command. One of them held a roll written on the inside and on the outside. The angels asked each other who was fit to be trusted with it.

Some angels named one man, some another. Each time the answer was that these were holy and righteous, but not enough for this. They counted up many names of saints. At last they said that no one was fit for it except Ephrem, and they gave him the roll.

When the dreamer got up in the morning, he heard people saying that Ephrem was teaching. His words, they said, flowed from his mouth like water from a fountain. Then, it says, the old man knew within himself that the words coming from Ephrem's lips were of the Holy Spirit.

The second dream is one Ephrem himself is said to have had as a youth. A vine grew out of his tongue and filled the whole space beneath the heavens, loaded with clusters of grapes. All the birds of heaven came and ate from it. The whole time they ate, the clusters grew in number and in size.
documented_stories.title: Two Dreams About Ephrem
documented_stories.when: undated, within Ephrem's life of about 306 to 373; the second dream is from his youth

documented_stories.teaser: Before dawn at Nisibis, men and women of the covenant gather for the vigil. The daughters of the covenant sing a teaching hymn, and the Gospel is read as one story.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a typical morning gathering as it would have gone - offered openly as reconstruction, never as a remembered event
documented_stories.telling:
Before dawn in Nisibis, those bound by the covenant gather for the vigil. No single morning like this was written down. This one is pieced together from separate sources, from the years before the city was handed to Persia in 363.

The covenanters are men and women who have taken the vow and stay unmarried. They walk through the dark streets from their own family houses, since there is no cloister. Among them stands the choir of the daughters of the covenant, who will raise the madrasha, the teaching hymn.

The hymn carries the teaching on its tune, stanza answering refrain, until the whole gathering holds the argument by heart. The Gospel read out is the harmony, the Gospels woven into one unbroken story.

The feast this season keeps the Lord's birth and his baptism together in one observance, as this city then did. When the light is full, the covenanters keep their fast and go back to their own households and their work in town.
documented_stories.title: A Morning of the Covenant at Nisibis
documented_stories.when: 337 to 363 (a typical morning built from separate sources, not one recorded day)

documented_stories.teaser: Theodoret wrote about a century later. He says Jacob of Nisibis cursed the Persians with nothing worse than gnats and mosquitoes. In his telling, the Persians fled.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the city's remembered deliverance - Jacob's prayer on the wall, as the church told it
documented_stories.telling:
Ephrem's hymns sing that Nisibis was saved when Shapur, king of Persia, laid siege to it. They say nothing of gnats. The story of Jacob's prayer comes from Theodoret of Cyrus, a Greek church historian, writing about a century later. Even the siege it belongs to is unsettled, whether that of 338, 346 or 350.

Shapur's army lay against the walls, and the river had been turned against the city. In Theodoret's telling, Ephrem begged the aged bishop Jacob to go up on the wall and curse the enemy. The old man agreed and climbed into a tower, where he looked out over the numberless camp.

Then, Theodoret writes, "he called down no other curse on them than that mosquitoes and gnats should be sent against them." Clouds of them came after his prayer and drove the elephants and the horses wild, until the Persians left their camp and fled.
documented_stories.title: Jacob of Nisibis and the Siege

documented_stories.teaser: The tradition tells that Simeon, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, is brought in chains before King Shapur. He will not worship the sun, and he is put to death with his clergy.
documented_stories.tellable_as: how the Persian church remembered its bishop's death, as the tradition tells it
documented_stories.telling:
"As time went on, the Christians grew in number. They began to form churches, and they appointed priests and deacons." So Sozomen, a Greek historian of the fifth century, opens his account of the persecution in Persia. The Magi, the priestly guardians of the Persian religion, grew deeply angry.

Simeon was bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, the royal cities of Persia, and he was accused of being a friend of the Roman emperor. King Shapur laid heavy taxes on the Christians, hoping poverty would force them to give up their faith. The year of what followed is disputed, 341 or about 344.

The tradition tells that Simeon was brought before the king in chains and would not bow down. He said he stood there now in defense of godliness and of our faith. Shapur offered him gifts, then threatened to destroy him and all the Christians. Each time Simeon refused to worship the sun or betray his religion.

As Simeon was led to prison, Usthazanes, the king's aged foster-father, rose to honor him. Usthazanes had been a Christian, but he had given way and worshipped the sun. The bishop rebuked him and turned his face away. Usthazanes then confessed himself a Christian before the king, and Shapur had him beheaded.

The next day Simeon again refused to worship the king or the sun. A hundred other prisoners were put to death that day while he watched. Simeon was killed last of all, with two aged priests of his own church.
documented_stories.title: Simeon Before the King of Persia
documented_stories.when: 341 by the traditional count (some argue about 344)

documented_stories.teaser: A later Life of Ephrem says a vision sends him to meet Basil, who ordains him a deacon. Basil never names the Syrian he praises, and the meeting is a later legend.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a beloved later legend, told with its correction attached - only when a participant raises it
documented_stories.telling:
Ephrem's fame reached the Greek church in his own century. Sozomen, a Greek historian of the next century, writes that Basil greatly admired him and was astonished at his learning. Basil later became bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Palladius of Galatia and Jerome both name Ephrem a deacon of the church at Edessa.

A later age built a meeting on a passage in Basil's own writings. There Basil credits an explanation of Scripture to an unnamed Syrian. He says the Syrian knew little of worldly wisdom but much of the knowledge of the Truth.

Later tradition took that Syrian to be Ephrem. Basil never names him, and he may well be another man, Eusebius of Emesa. The meeting itself is a later legend.

The later Life of Ephrem tells the story with love for both men. A vision prompted the poet to travel to Caesarea to see the great Basil. The two holy men had no common language, yet they recognized each other in the Spirit. And Basil himself, the Life says, ordained Ephrem a deacon.
documented_stories.title: The Meeting of Ephrem and Basil
documented_stories.when: set in Ephrem's lifetime, between 340 and 373 (a later legend)

documented_stories.teaser: A later tradition says Ephrem founded the choirs of the daughters of the covenant. In his own time, we know only that these women sang his hymns.
documented_stories.tellable_as: what later people said about how the hymns reached the whole church, told as later memory and not as fact from our own time
documented_stories.telling:
The daughters of the covenant sang the madrashe, our teaching hymns, in the churches of our own years. That much our own time attests.

How their choirs began is a story from the next age. Jacob of Serug told it in a verse homily around the year 500, more than a century after Ephrem died. Only that later memory says Ephrem himself founded and led the choirs.

In Jacob's telling, the people of Edessa were charmed by the songs of Bardaisan, a philosopher of Edessa's royal court. They were charmed as well by the songs of Mani, who founded a new religion. So Ephrem gathered the daughters of the covenant and taught them to sing true teaching in the same sweet forms. Through the women's voices, his teaching reached the whole city, women and men alike.
documented_stories.title: Ephrem and the Women's Choirs
documented_stories.when: 340 to 373 (first told about 500, more than a century after Ephrem's death)

documented_stories.teaser: Palladius and Sozomen tell that in Edessa's famine, Ephrem takes money from the rich and sets up some three hundred beds. He nurses the starving until the famine ends, and he dies within a month.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the remembered account of how Ephrem spent his last year, as the early tradition tells it
documented_stories.telling:
In the last year of Ephrem's life, famine struck Edessa. Palladius of Galatia and Sozomen, a Greek historian, both tell of that year, writing a generation and more after his death. Their count of beds and the words they report come from remembered tradition.

For many years Ephrem had lived quietly in his cell, but now he left it and went to the rich of the city. He asked them why they had no pity on people dying around them, while their wealth spoiled into the condemnation of their own souls.

The rich answered that they had no one they could trust with the giving, because everyone was dishonest in such business. Ephrem asked what they thought of him, and they said they knew him to be a man of God. "Then trust me," he said. "See, on your behalf I appoint myself to take in and care for the needy."

He took their money and set up some three hundred beds in the public porches. There he nursed the starving and the sick, strangers and local people alike, and he buried those who died. When the year was over and good times returned, he went back to his cell. He died soon after, a month later in Palladius's account and a few days later in Sozomen's.
documented_stories.title: Ephrem Leaves His Cell for the Famine

floor_note.text: This world held the same faith the Nicene Council put into words. One of its own bishops, Jacob of Nisibis, signed that creed himself in 325. But this world's native language for its faith was not a philosopher's definition - it was praise, sung more than argued. One figure connected to this world, the philosopher-poet Bardaisan, makes the question harder. He argued for free will exactly as this world did. But on whether the body itself is raised from the dead, the best modern reading finds that his own teaching most likely diverged from this world's confession. Exactly where he stood, in the end, is a question this world's own record leaves open.

The language of these churches. Ephrem wrote hymns in it. Aphrahat's first twenty-two letters each begin with the next letter of its alphabet.

The covenant. Men and women took a lifelong vow to stay unmarried. They lived in their towns and served the congregation.
The plural of ihidaya, the Single One. The word names a vowed celibate. It is also a title of Christ, the Only-Begotten.

A deacon and poet who taught the faith in hymns. He lived at Nisibis until 363 and then at Edessa, where he died in 373.
A teacher who wrote inside the Persian empire. His twenty-three letters survive, dated 336 to 345. Outside them, nothing is known of his life.

A philosopher at the court of Abgar VIII of Edessa, 154 to 222. His words survive only in a student's dialogue and in Ephrem's replies.
A teacher who rejected the Maker of the world. Churches that followed him shared the region in these years.

The Persian king whose persecution of Christians began in the 340s.

A bishop of the royal city, put to death under Shapur II. The traditional date is 341. Some scholars argue for about 344.
A bishop killed in the persecution. After his death the chief seat in Persia stood empty for about twenty years.
A bishop in Roman Mesopotamia. He went to the Persian court as an envoy. Later stories tell of miracles on his visits.
The Persian king who gave royal permission for the synod of 410.
The man the bishops at Nicaea in 325 met to answer. Those who answered him confessed the Son as true God.

A church historian, about 393 to about 460. He told of Jacob and the gnats about a century after the sieges.
A church writer who died about 430. His account of Ephrem's last year was written about 420.

legacy.text: This world's own woven Gospel did not last forever. Within a generation of this world's close, a new translation split the four Gospels apart again. Tradition credits Bishop Rabbula of Edessa with the change. But this world's own record leaves open how much of it was really his doing. Once the harmony stopped being copied, the original Syriac text itself did not survive. It is known today only through fragments, quotations, and translations made from it in other languages.

read_first.note: This world's greatest hymn-writer remembering the siege of his own city and its bishops in verse - the closest thing this world has to an eyewitness account, and sung rather than told.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in hymns and doctrinal teaching. Ephrem's enormous corpus stands first, then Aphrahat's twenty-three dated Demonstrations. It is also strong on the persecution as it was lived on the Persian side, and on the frontier cities' own civic memory. It thins out, and sometimes falls silent, in a few places. Ordinary believers never speak in their own words. The daughters of the covenant sang in every church, but their own voices do not survive - only men's writing about them does. Aphrahat's dispute with his Jewish neighbors is recorded only from his own side. Anyone enslaved, or of low status, left no voice at all. The years after Ephrem's death in 373 thin out fast too, down to little more than a list of bishops.

story.text: From about 200 to 410 CE, Syriac-speaking Christians lived on the frontier between the Roman and Persian empires. Edessa lay under Roman rule, though its people spoke Aramaic. Nisibis was a Roman fortress city from 298 until Rome gave it up to Persia in 363. Aphrahat wrote his letters from inside Persia. The city chronicle of Edessa holds the earliest trace of a church there. Written about 340 years later, it says a flood in about 201 destroyed a church building. Scholars dispute whether that line is original.

These Christians taught through song and symbol. Ephrem, a deacon, wrote teaching hymns called madrashe. Each had a refrain, so a congregation learned the faith by singing it. He read Scripture and the world through the raza, a symbol bound to the truth it shows. In this reading, Eden answers the cross, and the Jordan answers the font of baptism. In his Pearl hymns, he reads a whole theology out of one pearl. The first hymn begins, "One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl."

These churches heard the Gospel as one continuous story. Around 172, a man named Tatian wove Matthew, Mark, Luke and John into a single harmony. Aphrahat quotes it, and Ephrem wrote a commentary on it.

At the core of the community's vowed life stood the covenant, called the qyama. Its members were men and women who promised to stay unmarried for life and to serve the congregation. They lived in town, among their own families. Aphrahat's sixth Demonstration, from 337, is the earliest dated witness. It speaks to an order already in place. Members were also called ihidaye, a word that means single ones. The same word is the Syriac title for Christ, the Only-Begotten. Ephrem's hymns show that women of the covenant sang them in choirs.

Who held authority was never settled in these years. Bishops led their churches. The vowed men and women of the covenant had a standing of their own. A trusted teacher also carried weight. Aphrahat drafted a letter for a meeting of bishops and clergy. Whether he was a bishop is unknown. In Persia, Papa claimed to lead all the bishops. He was bishop of the royal city of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. According to later chronicles, other bishops fiercely contested his claim around 315.

Ephrem also defined the faith by answering rivals who preached in the same cities and the same language. Bardaisan was a thinker at the court of the king of Edessa. His following lasted for two centuries after his death. Marcion rejected the Maker of the world, and his followers lived in the same region. Mani started a new religion in the third century. Ephrem answered all three by name, in prose and in hymns. He treated them as one kind of deception, though their systems were different.

On the Persian side, faith meant endurance under a hostile crown. In the 340s, King Shapur II turned on his Christian subjects. Sozomen, a church historian of the 400s, says Shapur first taxed them heavily and then had their priests killed. Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, was accused of siding with Rome. He refused to worship the sun and was executed with his clergy. Tradition dates his death to 341, and some scholars argue for about 344. Bishop after bishop was killed. After Barba'shmin, a later bishop, was killed, the church's chief seat in Persia stayed empty for about twenty years. Roman Edessa was largely without this persecution.

Around 400, Marutha went to the Persian court. He was a bishop in Roman Mesopotamia, sent as the Roman emperor's envoy. His access to King Yazdegerd I helped win royal permission for the synod of 410. The Persian state recognized the church that year. The synod set it in order as one body, with provinces under Isaac, bishop of the royal city.

dates.born: c. 306 (scholarly convention; Nisibis or its territory, per Sozomen)
dates.died: 373, at Edessa (Jerome: 'died in the reign of Valens'; the famine-relief tradition places his last public act shortly before)
dates.floruit: Nisibis until the 363 cession, then Edessa 363-373; deacon (Jerome De viris; Palladius; Griffith 1986)

voices.hedge: A later tradition, composed more than a century after his death, credits Ephrem with personally founding and leading the women's choirs that sang his hymns. This world's own record attests only that the choirs performed the hymns - not that Ephrem organized them himself.
voices.text: Ephrem was a deacon, first at Nisibis and then, after 363, at Edessa - and this world's most prolific poet. Hundreds of his teaching hymns carried this world's doctrine straight into congregational song. In the last year of his life, famine struck Edessa. He came out of his quiet cell, took charge of relief for the whole city, and died within a month of the famine's end.

dates.died: 338 vs 350 - the Martyrologium Hieronymianum implies 338 (the first siege), the Chronicon Paschale has him defending Nisibis in 350; a genuine primary-source conflict, held open and never resolved either way
dates.floruit: bishop of Nisibis from c. 309; signatory at Nicaea (325); the city's remembered intercessor in the Persian siege tradition (which siege is open); traditionally Ephrem's own bishop and baptizer

names.name: Jacob of Nisibis (bishop from c. 309; at Nicaea 325; died 338 or 350 - a genuine primary-source conflict)

voices.hedge: This world's own record cannot even agree on when Jacob died - one chronicle says 338, during the first siege; another has him still defending the city in 350. The gnat-swarm detail itself comes from a historian writing about a century afterward; Ephrem's own hymns, written at the time, describe the same deliverance without it.
voices.text: Jacob was bishop of Nisibis from about 309. He signed the Nicene Creed himself, at the council in 325. When a Persian army besieged his city, tradition remembers him climbing the wall to pray. He prayed not for the army's destruction, but for its withdrawal.

dates.floruit: bishop in Roman Mesopotamia; envoy between the Roman court and Yazdegerd I; his access helped secure royal permission for the synod of 410

names.name: Marutha, bishop in Roman Mesopotamia and imperial envoy to Yazdegerd I (fl. c. 399-410s)

voices.hedge: The surviving account of his embassies includes miracle elements - a cured headache, an exposed fraud - told in the church's own memory of him, not as verified reporting.
voices.text: Marutha was a Roman bishop on the frontier. His embassies to the Persian court helped open the way to a lasting settlement. His diplomacy with King Yazdegerd I helped bring about the synod of 410. That synod finally gave the Persian church one settled structure.

dates.died: traditionally 341; Kosinski and Burgess argue c. 344 - the anchor date for the whole chronicle-derived succession, held open and never resolved either way
dates.floruit: bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the opening of the Great Persecution

names.name: Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon (martyred under Shapur II; traditional date 341, disputed - c. 344 argued)

voices.hedge: The year of his death is genuinely disputed - 341 by the traditional count, with some historians arguing for about 344 instead - and the fullest surviving account of his martyrdom is a Greek historian's reworking of the original Syriac tradition, written decades later.
voices.text: Simeon bar Sabbae was bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. King Shapur II ordered Persia's Christians taxed into ruin. Simeon refused to collect that tax. He also refused to worship the sun. He was executed along with his own clergy. This world remembers him as the first of the persecution's bishops to die for the faith.

tile.text: Between about 200 and 410, Syriac-speaking Christians lived in the frontier country between the Roman and Persian empires, at Edessa and Nisibis. A city chronicle written long afterward says a flood in about 201 destroyed a church building at Edessa. These Christians taught the faith through hymns and symbols. They heard the Gospel as one continuous story, woven from the four by a man named Tatian. Men and women of the covenant promised to stay unmarried for life, and they lived in town among their families. Ephrem, a deacon, answered the rival teachers Bardaisan, Marcion and Mani by name. Bishops led, yet covenant members and trusted teachers also held standing, and these churches never settled which counted most. In the 340s, King Shapur II turned on the Christians of Persia, and bishop after bishop was killed. The church's chief seat there later stood empty for about twenty years. At the synod of 410, the Persian church was set in order as one body.
